Behavioral capabilities

Between 2 and 3 years, behavior shifts from mostly reactive, here-and-now routines to planned, symbolic, and increasingly rule-governed performance across domains. Around 24 months, children often speak in telegraphic two-word phrases (e.g. "mommy go"); soon after, they undergo a vocabulary burst. Expressive vocabulary grows from on the order of tens of words at age 2 to hundreds by age 3. By 30 months, most toddlers know at least  50 words (some know many more), and by 36 months vocabularies of several hundred to 1000 words are common. Toddlers begin combining words into longer utterances–by three years they routinely use 3-4 word sentences. Their grammar is still immature (omitting or misusing some particles and tenses), but they start using basic pronouns and plurals correctly. Receptive language also expands: two-year-olds can follow one-step commands; by 3 they understand two- to three-step instructions and spatial terms like "in," "on," and "under" 1. They can name familiar objects and even tell you their own name and gender. Three-year-olds typically ( 75% of the time 2) speak clearly enough that unfamiliar adults understand most of what they say, and they can carry on a simple conversation with a few back-and-forth exchanges.

Although far from fully mature, the roots of executive function are increasingly observable during this stage. Between 2-3 years, children show improvements in attention span and working memory, enabling them to hold in mind and follow multi-step (typically 2-step but often 3-step 1) commands and simple routines. They also begin exerting inhibitory control over impulses in certain contexts; a two-year-old might grab a treat as soon as they see it, whereas a three-year-old is slightly more likely to wait when told "not yet". Caregivers still provide crucial external regulation (reminders, rules, distraction), but toddlers internalize some of these rules over time. By the end of this period, many children can plan a multi-step play activity (like building a specific tower out of blocks) with minimal adult help, showing emerging ability to organize actions towards a goal 3.

By 2 years, most children walk and run with ease; over the next year their mobility and coordination improve markedly. By around 36 months, toddlers can run and climb confidently, jump in place, and even pedal a tricycle. They also begin walking up and down stairs with an alternating foot pattern (one foot per step) instead of the earlier one-step-at-a-time method 4. Hand-eye coordination and dexterity also advance. A 1- to 2-year-old can usually stack a few blocks; by 3 years, children build towers of more than six blocks and manipulate small objects with greater precision; they can coordinate both hands to string large beads, turn book pages one at a time, and start to copy simple shapes (e.g. drawing a circle). Improved fine motor control allows for more self-care (e.g. feeding with a spoon/fork, beginning to dress/undress) and tool use.

One of the hallmark changes in this period is the blossoming of symbolic thought (the ability to let one thing represent another in the mind). Around the second birthday, toddlers begin to engage in pretend play: for example, using a block as a "phone" or "feeding" a doll with an empty spoon; as they approach 3 years, pretend play becomes more elaborate and imaginative 5. Children start acting out scenarios with themes and roles, such as playing house or pretending to be animals and characters. They also demonstrate early visual-artistic symbolism: for example, a three-year-old can copy a circle or cross with crayon, and will often ascribe meaning to their drawings ("This is Mommy") even if abstract. It should be noted that at this age the line between fantasy and reality can be blurry; a 3-year-old may believe their pretend monsters are real and become afraid, since the cognitive ability to reliably distinguish imagination from reality will develop closer to age 4 5.

Alongside pretend play, causal, numerical, and spatial reasoning all take practical leaps. A toddler at 2 might trial-and-error with simple cause-and-effect toys; by 3 they confidently operate toys with buttons, levers, and moving parts to produce intended effects 1. In "blicket detector"-style tasks, 2-3-year-olds infer novel causal relations from sparse covariation and interventions 6 and explore more when evidence is confounded 7. They can also work on easy puzzles (3-4 pieces) 1 and, numerically, many children move from rote counts to being "subset-knowers" who can map small number words onto exact set sizes, with full grasp of the cardinality principle emerging for many slightly after this window; still, by  3 years they often answer "how many?" correctly for small sets.

Socially, 2-to-3-year-olds move beyond solitary and parallel play into more interactive engagements. Imitation is a powerful tool at this age - children copy the actions of adults and peers, learning social routines and basic cultural behaviors 1. They show emerging empathy and attachment: a toddler may spontaneously show affection to friends (e.g. hugging a playmate) and express concern if a peer is crying or upset, reflecting the beginnings of reliable social perspective-taking 1. By 3 years, children start to engage in simple cooperative play. They can take turns in games (though patience is limited) and are learning to share, at least in structured situations 5. Possessiveness peaks during the "terrible twos" ("mine!" is a favorite word), but gradually they come to understand the property rights of others. Emotionally, toddlers display a wide range of feelings and quick mood shifts. Frustration and inability to communicate effectively at age 2 often lead to temper tantrums (screaming, crying, even breath-holding). By around 3, as language and self-control improve, many children handle emotions slightly better - they may use words to protest or seek comfort from adults instead of only throwing fits. They also separate more easily from parents at this age, showing that secure attachment and confidence in exploring have increased. Still, changes in routine can upset a 3-year-old, and they thrive on consistency and reassurance as they develop coping skills.

Development of episodic and autobiographical memory: The importance of remembering forgetting

Training data and optimization

In the 2-3 year window, the brain is effectively pursuing a handful of coupled optimization problems at once, and each has a characteristic stream of "training data" and error routing that drives the aforementioned behavioral gains. For language, the objective is to compress and generalize lexical-syntactic regularities while minimizing pragmatic failure; dense child-directed speech and joint-attention episodes generate layer-by-layer cortical prediction errors (surprisal at the next phoneme/word/morpheme) that reshape representations, while communicative success/failure yields dopaminergic reward-prediction errors (approval, repair, being understood vs not) that reinforce production choices and conversational policy; apical dendritic plateaus gate when those local errors "write," and offline replay consolidates them, resulting in the vocabulary burst and first combinatorial grammar.

Building directly on the 12-24-month spatial learning algorithm, the 2-3 year objective shifts from merely reorienting to actively stabilizing and extending a queryable scene-graph that binds who-what-where-when across delays, viewpoints, and displacements. The optimizer still closes self-motion drift against extended surfaces, but now it reliability-weights multiple cues (geometry, gateways/corners, and distinctive landmarks) by their stability and distinctiveness, so that boundary-anchored grids reset phase, item features attach to LEC-like codes, and retrosplenial/AG hubs improve the egocentric-allocentric transform at room transitions. Training data are the errors that arise at loop closure and displacement: returning to a start point and being "off," failing to predict which doorway leads to a hidden target, misbinding an object to a look-alike corner, or retrieving an episode and landing at the wrong heading. These mismatches drive novelty/comparator signals in DG-CA3-CA1, tag active assemblies (including large apical Ca2+ plateaus/BTSP-like events), and prioritize them for offline replay, which stitches short trajectories into longer routes and cements landmark-geometry conjuncts. With each tagged-and-replayed episode, objects, corners, and gateways consolidate as graph nodes, transitions as edges, and place codes become more viewpoint-invariant; language labels for relations ("in/on/under," "by the door") begin to cue retrieval, further reducing search entropy.

For social valuation, the toddler is tuning a composite objective that weighs self-reward, concern for others’ outcomes, and compliance with simple rules. The data stream is dense and scalar: praise, smiles, touch, approving words, and access to peers act as positive reward-prediction errors; reprimands, withdrawal of attention, and brief "time-outs" act as negative ones; witnessing another’s need or failed goal generates vicarious errors. These signals train orbitofrontal/vmPFC-ventral striatum loops to recalibrate the value of social actions, while dACC/insula register others’ distress and norm conflict to engage control. TPJ/STS sharpen inverse-planning over others’ goals so credit assignment lands on the right features (who needed help, which rule applied). Serotonin lengthens the time horizon and raises the subjective cost of impulsive grabs, promoting patience and turn-taking; norepinephrine adjusts learning rates in volatile settings (new peer, new room); oxytocin/vasopressin increase the gain on affiliative cues so approval becomes a stronger teacher. Language supplies crisp rule tokens ("share," "wait," "no hitting"), letting basal-ganglia gates cache deontic policies that generalize. During sleep, hippocampal-cortical replay prioritizes episodes where helping or fair play yielded rich approval, strengthening other-regarding and norm weights. The readout between 2-3 years (more spontaneous helping, proto-fairness, emerging reputation sensitivity, longer turn-taking without prompts) falls out naturally from this training loop. The family-play study examines associations among play measures (Figure) 23.

For tool use, the objective is learning controllable cause-effect structure to achieve a comfortable, functional end state. Toddlers aren’t just repeating motor synergies; they’re discovering which interventions on objects (and on their own joints) reliably produce the desired distal outcome while leaving the body in a viable final posture. When a reach-grasp-transport ends in an awkward or unstable configuration (e.g wrist over-rotated, elbow locked, handle oriented wrong), the proprioceptive and vestibular mismatch, elevated effort, and micro-failures at contact yield large cerebellar teaching signals (climbing-fiber spikes) plus fronto-striatal negative TD-errors. Those errors update inverse models toward anticipatory pre-shaping and correct grip selection, and they also reshape the "policy over interventions" so the child chooses levers, rakes, or handles that make the end state easy. Conversely, successful, low-effort end states deliver positive TD-errors and lower cerebellar error, reinforcing the whole action sequence and the specific causal belief ("this action with this orientation causes that outcome"). Over weeks of practice, the system shifts from brute force to planning: the hand rotates before contact, the body chooses a stance that affords the terminal wrist angle, and the child selects the right implement geometry on the first try because the causal model now predicts which action will yield a high-comfort terminal pose. Recent naturalistic observations show object engagement becoming more frequent, sustained, and complex with age (Figure) 20. The same study links toddlers’ object engagement to social opportunity and outdoor settings (Figure). A 2026 study classifies children’s object engagement (Figure).

The gross motor objective factorizes into precision, efficiency, and vigor. Dense, self-initiated practice yields tightly time-locked error that cerebellar complex spikes use to train forward/inverse models, cutting endpoint variance, anticipating load, and pre-shaping grasp; in parallel, corticospinal myelination and synergy pruning (the process by which broad, overlapping motor patterns (or "synergies") are gradually refined into more precise, independent control of muscles and joints) increase bandwidth to distal musculature. Basal ganglia learn an effort-time trade-off, with tonic dopamine setting average vigor as opportunity cost so movements become quicker yet smoother, with fewer corrective submovements and earlier anticipatory postural adjustments. The altered nature of motor objectives is reflected behaviorally as step-to stair climbing gives way to alternating gait, running and pedaling stabilize, hand aperture scales with object size before contact, and utensil trajectories straighten, approaching Fitts-like speed-accuracy efficiency (i.e. movements converge toward the law that faster actions require reduced accuracy, and accuracy requires slower, more carefully controlled movements) in everyday reaches.

For emerging executive control, the objective is to maintain a task state and suppress prepotent actions, which is common across tasks regardless of domain; multi-step instructions, turn-taking games, and A-not-B/detour-like conflicts deliver negative and positive TD errors into cortico-striatal loops, tuning working-memory gating and inhibitory policy, with ACh/NE adjusting precision and learning rates under stable vs volatile contexts-so toddlers get noticeably better at waiting, following 2-3-step routines, and organizing play toward a goal. A 2026 study examines executive function in two-year-olds (Figure) 24. The study compares executive function with fine motor skills (Figure).

Pretend play is the toddler’s sandbox: it trains event schemas by having the child actively compose agents, roles, goals, and causal contingencies into coherent episodes. By staging counterfactuals ("the block is a phone," "I’m the doctor"), hippocampal-DMN-PFC loops practice event segmentation, role binding, and temporal ordering, yielding reusable narrative priors (scripts with slots for agents, tools, locations, and goals) that later scaffold narrative comprehension and multi-step planning (along with providing a fruitful activity to engage in with other agents). This synergizes with imitation: demonstrations supply grounded action sketches, while pretense expands them combinatorially, so policy search in new tasks starts with both a motor scaffold and a narrative scaffold for predicting who does what, when, and why; this speaks to a deeper truth about human learning: humans’ capacity for generalization is perhaps largely due to the uniquely human propensity to take what information/episodes are available and to generate expansive learning signals based on counterfactual simulations. A 2026 study observes toddler symbolic play with family (Figure). The study compares symbolic play across interaction conditions (Figure).

Fundamental drives for curiosity/uncertainty resolution sit over all of this: toddlers continue to preferentially sample the "Goldilocks" band where prediction errors are informative yet tractable, and neuromodulators schedule when to exploit a stable model (ACh-weighted precision), reset it under volatility (NE), or invest effort/patience (5-HT) while distributional dopamine supplies signed updates. Imitation also remains an underlying meta-objective that accelerates learning curves.

Neural development

From a neurocomputational standpoint, ages 24-36 months mark the high-plasticity summit of the human cortex precisely as the system retools for efficiency. Regionally staggered synaptogenesis has pushed association cortex to its most exuberant state: classic quantitative work shows that primary sensory cortices peak earlier (within the first year), whereas prefrontal association cortex crests around  3-3.5 years at nearly double adult synaptic density before protracted pruning ensues 9. Converging cellular evidence shows that dendritic spine densities in human prefrontal cortex during childhood exceed adult values by roughly two- to three-fold and only begin their prolonged decline during puberty, continuing to remodel through the third decade 10. The metabolic footprint matches this exuberance: developmental PET work demonstrates a marked rise to a childhood hypermetabolic plateau, with cortical glucose utilization around early preschool years substantially above ( 2x) adult levels 11.

Morphometrically, absolute gray-matter expansion has largely crested by  18-24 months; after that point, "apparent thinning" of cortex reflects intracortical myelination and pruning rather than degeneration per se. Longitudinal infant/toddler MRI shows cortical thickness and volume rising rapidly in year one, flattening by year two 12, and then trending downwards in early childhood 13, while quantitative and biophysical MRI link the thickness decline specifically to increasing myelin within the cortical ribbon 13. Functionally, this shortens local integration windows and reduces energy per transmitted bit, shifting the system from diffuse local coupling to more selective, gated interactions that favor policy stabilization over reflexive responses.

White-matter organization continues its steep, tract-specific efficiency gains through toddlerhood. Longitudinal diffusion work across birth-to-6 years shows rising fractional anisotropy with falling radial diffusivity across major association bundles, indicating thicker sheaths and tighter axonal packing 14; individual differences by age one are already predictive of microstructure at six, implying early-established "throughput budgets". In perisylvian language-control loops, these microstructural improvements are especially salient: dorsal (arcuate) and lateral frontoparietal (SLF II/III) segments show measurable maturation across the preschool window 14, and independent studies linking the richness of early conversational turn-taking through age two to stronger myelination in language tracts by toddlerhood 15. These changes lengthen the brain’s effective communication radius at a roughly fixed energy budget, enabling faster top-down selection and tighter perception-action coupling.

At the systems level, large-scale networks continue to be more recognizable and less spatially diffuse than in infancy. During natural sleep, 1.5-3.5-year-olds already express a familiar set of intrinsic networks; within this window, posterior default-mode components become more reliable and track developmental skills, and language/salience networks sharpen in children with stronger behavioral scores 16. Anticorrelation between default-mode and dorsal attention networks (characteristic of adult "internal-model vs. control" arbitration) remains weak but trends in the expected direction 17, supported by increasing perfusion to posterior midline hubs and ongoing tuning of thalamocortical relays that coordinate cortico-cortical communication. The net effect between 24-36 months is more stable event-modeling at rest and quicker, more selective recruitment of control networks during tasks. A recent study maps functional networks in children under five (Figure) 21. A 2026 peer-reviewed study maps population-level network organization across toddlerhood (Figure) 22. The same study tests how individualized boundaries change estimates of within-network connectivity (Figure). The study maps variation in network location (Figure).

Spectrally, the system continues to point towards tighter excitation-inhibition control and faster sampling. Across  24-36 months there is a continued shift from dominant theta toward rising alpha/mu power, a flattening of the aperiodic 1/f slope, and a gradual increase of peak-alpha frequency 18. Sleep physiology gives a concordant readout of thalamocortical maturity: between age two and three, spindles lengthen and densify and slow/fast spindle topographies begin to differentiate 19.

Pulling these threads together, the 2-3 window is a hinge point where exuberant synaptic resources meet rapidly improving conduction and gating, under a metabolic regime that is generous but beginning a multi-year transition towards adult-level efficiency. The macro-result is a brain that can sustain more selective, longer-range, lower-cost communication; stabilize latent event models at rest; and pivot control more quickly during tasks, all of which shows up behaviorally as sharper turn-taking and articulation planning, longer working-memory spans for action sequences, and more deliberate tool-mediated manipulation.
